name: Wei Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I run an underground loader at the Greystone zinc and lead mine, a big low-slung machine that scoops broken rock from the stopes, which are the open spaces where the ore's been blasted, and carries it to the ore pass. We go down in the cage at six, get the briefing at the crib room on level 8, and then it's mucking all shift, bucket after bucket, in the dust and the noise with the lights on my helmet. I've been at it about eighteen months, so I'm still the guy they give the easy headings to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew, honestly. There's an older operator, Lionel, who taught me how to feel the bucket when it's full without looking, and that felt like being let into a secret. What wears me out is the heat on the deep levels and the hours, because my partner Ana is a nurse on rotating shifts, so some weeks we only see each other asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that actually matters, like ventilation on level 10 and the roster. At work everyone would laugh about all the hype. Online I might share a joke about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep learning the job and saving for a place with Ana. We've got about ten months of costs put away and my car is paid off, so we're not in a rush. If nothing changes, the plan stays the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep putting money into the house deposit account each fortnight, keep turning up, and ask the shift boss about getting signed off on the bigger loader. I'd stay in the union and maybe go to a few more meetings about the heat on the deep levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small stuff. I used one to help write a complaint letter about our rent going up, and Ana uses it to check drug names sometimes. Never at work, there's no signal underground anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still nag at you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tele-remote trial on level 6. They've got one loader being driven from a chair on the surface already, and that's got nothing to do with AI hype. So even in the boring version, I'd want to know where that's heading.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what actually matters, like the ventilation on level 10 and the roster. At work we'd laugh about the hype.
S0.think: It means I keep learning the job and saving for a place with Ana. We have about ten months of costs saved and the car is paid off, so the plan stays the plan.
S0.do: Keeps paying into the house deposit every fortnight and asks to be signed off on the bigger loader. Stays in the union and goes to more meetings about heat on the deep levels.
S0.quote: They've got one loader being driven from a chair on the surface already, and that's got nothing to do with AI hype.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is relaxed and practical, with his eyes on a house deposit. Even when told AI is hype, he points to the tele-remote trial already running in his mine. He separates the AI story from the automation he can see with his own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table for every change, and the people who lose tasks should be first in line for the new ones. At work I'd back the reps. Online I'd share stuff about fair transition, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the loader job goes tele-remote within a few years, and that's not the end of the world for me. If Lionel and the others go first and it works, I'd follow. Being on the surface instead of 900 metres down wouldn't break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the experienced guys had done the tele-remote course and then put my name down, probably within the first six months. I'd go to the union meetings and push for the course to be paid, on paid time. And I'd keep saving the deposit as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly curious. It's change, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company roll out stuff that didn't work. They gave us tablets for the prestart checks and half of them died in the first month from the dust. I'd rather Lionel tells me it's real before I bet my roster on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older contractors who aren't in the union and just do the night shifts. They don't get offered courses, they just don't get called back. That's who gets dropped quietly.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table, and people who lose tasks should be first in line for the new jobs. I'd back the reps and share things about a fair transition.
S1.think: I think the loader job goes tele-remote within a few years, and that isn't the end of the world. If it works for the older operators, I'd follow and be glad to be on the surface.
S1.do: Waits until experienced operators have done the tele-remote course, then signs up within about six months. Pushes the union for paid training on paid time and keeps saving the house deposit.
S1.quote: They gave us tablets for the prestart checks and half of them died in the first month from the dust.
S1.fieldNote: His caution is earned from watching bad tech rollouts, not from fear of change. He's happy to move to the surface once it's proven. His worry goes outward to the non-union contractors he thinks will be dropped quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in hard and fast, with a basic income or something like it, because nobody's ready. I'd be telling everyone at work to stick together. Online I'd probably get into arguments, which I usually avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tele-remote chair goes too. If AI can drive the loader better than Lionel, it doesn't need me sitting on the surface watching it. And Ana's job isn't safe either if robots can do hands-on work, which is the part that really gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freeze the house plan straight away and keep the deposit as our safety money, because ten months of costs plus the deposit gets us a long way. I'd go to every union meeting and write to our member of parliament. If the job went, I'd sign up for whatever public support existed without feeling bad about it, that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lying-on-the-floor scared, because we've got money, but a weight that wouldn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With just two years' warning, what would those two years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me going to work every day knowing it's ending, and saving every cent. I don't think I'd retrain in two years, because what would I retrain for, if everything goes at once? I'd spend the time on getting the rules right, not on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana say to each other about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we'd rent a while longer and see. She'd be the calm one, she always is. She'd say people still need nurses until they don't, and we'd laugh at that because there's nothing else to do.

S2.say: I'd say governments need to step in hard and fast with something like a basic income, because nobody is ready. I'd tell everyone at work to stick together.
S2.think: I think even the tele-remote chair goes if AI can drive better than the best operator. What really gets me is that Ana's nursing isn't safe either if robots do hands-on work.
S2.do: Freezes the house purchase and keeps the deposit as safety money. Attends every union meeting, writes to his member of parliament, and would take public support without guilt if the job went.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a weight that won't lift, though savings keep it from turning into panic.
S2.quote: She'd say people still need nurses until they don't, and we'd laugh at that because there's nothing else to do.
S2.fieldNote: Money keeps him steady, but the threat to his partner's job hits harder than the threat to his own. He sees no point retraining with two years' notice and puts his energy into rules and collective pressure. He is comfortable relying on public support and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so let's use it for real transition plans, paid for by the companies that profit. At work I'd say the same thing, just with more swearing. I'd share whatever the union put out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough to get a trade ticket, but not enough to know which trade survives. I'd probably still go for it, because sitting still is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the tele-remote course and also start an electrical apprenticeship at night, if the union could get the company to chip in. I'd keep saving and hold off on the house until year two or three. Once it arrives, I'd lean on whatever the union and the government had set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Better than the two-year one, because I can see a few steps ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes it from waiting to doing. In two years I'd just hold on. In five, I could be a qualified sparky, I mean electrician, by the time it lands, and even if robots do wiring eventually, someone has to fix the robots first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. Is that fair on Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably say yes, she's the saver, not me. But I know she wants a garden. So maybe we'd buy something small and cheap, not the place on Hill Street we keep looking at.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a window for real transition plans, paid for by the companies that profit. I'd say the same at work and share what the union put out.
S3.think: Five years is long enough to get a trade ticket, but not long enough to know which trade survives. I'd still go for it, because sitting still is worse.
S3.do: Does the tele-remote course and starts a night-time electrical apprenticeship in the first year, ideally with company funding won by the union. Keeps saving and delays the house purchase by a year or two.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but better able to see a few steps ahead.
S3.quote: In five, I could be a qualified sparky, I mean electrician, by the time it lands, and even if robots do wiring eventually, someone has to fix the robots first.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns him from holding on to acting. His plan stacks a company course with a trade, while still leaning on the union to pay for it. He softens his house plan rather than dropping it, mindful of his partner's wishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so if people get left behind it's a choice someone made. I'd say that at work and online. I'd want the union pushing for a shorter work week rather than job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. I'd be thirty-seven, with a trade and probably a house. The end point is the same, but I'd have had time to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep the loader job, do the tele-remote course when the others have done it, and start looking at a trade properly instead of rushing. We'd probably buy the small house sooner, because ten years is time to pay a chunk off. I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the back of my head, but mostly fine. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right. Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, I suppose. Ana and I want them in a few years, and I don't know what I'd tell a kid about what to do for work in 2040. That's the bit no amount of planning fixes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay underground for most of those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few, yeah, because the pay's good and I'm only just getting decent. Lionel says it takes five years to be a real operator. I'd like to get there once, even if it doesn't last.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so leaving people behind would be a choice. I'd want the union pushing for a shorter work week instead of job cuts.
S4.think: I think I'd be all right, at thirty-seven with a trade and probably a house. The end point is the same, but I'd have time to get my feet under me.
S4.do: Keeps the loader job, takes the tele-remote course once proven, and researches a trade properly. Buys a small house sooner and votes for whoever has a plan for workers.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with some background unease about the future his children would face.
S4.quote: I don't know what I'd tell a kid about what to do for work in 2040.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his worry shifts from his own job to children he doesn't have yet. He wants to become a real operator once, even if it doesn't last, which shows pride in the craft. He frames any harm as a political choice, not fate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Ana's job goes in the same wave as mine and there's no time to plan. What would help is a basic income that's real, not a form you fill in every fortnight to prove you're looking for jobs that don't exist. And the union being part of the decisions, not reading about them after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. Underground is dangerous, people die. If a robot does the stopes, nobody's crushed by a rock fall, and I'd be lying if I said that wasn't a good thing. I just want the people who used to take that risk to get something out of it.

headlineQuote: If a robot does the stopes, nobody's crushed by a rock fall, and I'd be lying if I said that wasn't a good thing.
portrait: Wei Silva is a 27-year-old underground loader operator at a large zinc and lead mine, eighteen months into the job and still learning from an older operator named Lionel. He lives with his partner Ana, a nurse, and they are saving for a house with about ten months of costs set aside. He trusts change once others have tried it, and backs the union and public support. He stays calm when AI is hype, follows proven tele-remote work in the steady scenario, and grows anxious in the fast AGI picture mostly because his partner's job goes too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his partner's nursing job would go in the same wave as his and there would be no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A real basic income without fortnightly job-search forms, and the union taking part in decisions rather than hearing about them afterwards.
